title: A year into AI-assisted gamedev, I have one question: how are you handling regression testing in larger projects?
author: AppearanceEast2756
selftext:
I’ve been building a game in Unreal with AI for about a year. The development workflow has improved a lot, but regression testing is the part I’m actively working on now. I’d like to hear how people are handling it in larger projects.

Starting the full test suite and waiting for the results can already take around ten minutes. That adds up across short development cycles, and the current tests still don’t cover every mechanic.

I’m trying to make test selection more contextual by focusing on the systems I’m currently changing. But even that doesn’t feel efficient enough as a long-term approach, especially as the game keeps growing.

# A bit of context

I’m a longtime developer with a frontend background. This started as a side project and a way to learn how to work with AI. Along the way, I went through two major rewrites to make the workflow more manageable.

The first was moving the game logic from a mixed Blueprint/C++ setup into C++ and building my own MCP integration for Unreal.

The second was the UI, which had grown to more than 50 different screens, panels and dialogs. I built my own UI system using HTML-like templates, CSS and reusable components, connected to Unreal through a plugin and a native rendering layer. That gave the agents text files to edit and me a familiar workflow, Git diffs and hot reload for supported UI changes. It also meant rewriting the UI-related C++ integration across the game.

Both were substantial detours, but they removed a lot of recurring friction. Implementation became much easier to manage afterwards.

# What I can check now

My current setup has one orchestrator coordinating multiple agents. I also have developer commands that let me prepare the game state for testing.

For changes with a visible result, there’s a separate visual verification step after implementation. The checking agent gets the task requirements, written rules and screenshots from the running game. It compares the result against the requirements and the game’s visual style. If something doesn’t match, the task goes back for correction and another check.

This has saved me a lot of repetitive checking. I still play the game myself to judge how it feels and how progression works, but I don’t have to manually revisit every visible change.

The part I’m trying to improve now is checking what those changes might have broken elsewhere.

# How are you handling regression testing in larger projects?

I already have automated tests for the game logic and a visual verification step for new changes. What I’m trying to work out now is an efficient regression testing process that covers both.

That also means checking whether a change has broken other screens, UI states or the visible results of connected gameplay systems. Checking the element that was just changed is only part of the job. I still need a sensible way to decide what to revisit elsewhere in the game.

I’m interested in workflows people are actually using:

* How do you select logic tests and in-game scenarios to check visually again, including those indirectly affected by a change?
* How do you organise visual regression testing across different screens, UI states and gameplay situations? Are you using agents for that?
* When do you run the full set of tests and visual checks, and when do you limit them to selected areas?
* How do you expand coverage of mechanics and their visible results while keeping iteration reasonably quick?

This is what I’m working on right now. I’d appreciate concrete examples from larger projects, especially how you’re handling the visual side of regression testing. What has worked for you in practice?

P.S. If anyone wants to take a look at the game: [Calmaria: Wild Growth on Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4683860/Calmaria_Wild_Growth/).

comments.author: Zimgar
comments.body:
I mean it's hard?  This is why normal game studios typically still have human QA, because testing everything in automated ways is difficult.

Several game studios (even before AI), would create 'AI' that would play through their games.  Thus allowing them to regression test that way.  The Talos Principle series is a good example, very small team that did that well.  Had a couple GDC talks on it at one point.

Your asking not 'AI' knowledge questions, but more general how do you QA effectively.  I'd investigate that avenue and then apply that QA effectively knowledge to your AI scenario.

Here is what I'm doing atm, but you might already be doing this.  I have a suite of Developer Tools that can be run during runtime.  All features that are created for my game can be utilized through the Developer Tools, and via the game.  The Developer Tools always use the same logic as the game.  Each feature is then run through a series of tests from specific scenes, and can also be tested via the Developer Tool.

This covers testing everything in isolation at least.  For visual things screenshot tests generally workout well.   Then I have an AIBot setup that can play my game in an automated fashion.  This handles a decent amount of testing but mostly for logic bugs, not much for visual.    
  
Typically visual isolation tests cover most visual bugs.  It's usually a rare visual bug that doesn't show up in isolation but shows up in your full game.  (This does depend on type of game and features though... but glancing at your game I wouldn't think it would be an exception case).  
  
Hopefully this helps or makes sense?
